speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: I was trained and write it to another patient.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Would they work for their handout sometimes?

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: Some people asked them to work there. They had to do so or so. They gave you so and so. They would work there. Most of the years they gave free handouts. Probably not always.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: What kind of a town was Troy in the early days? Was it a pretty quiet little place?

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: Well, it went away from the times it wasn't so quiet. After they got the man for wood, that was shipped out. Then there was quite a bit of business. Then as time goes on, that's later. I remember that very well. When the pot lights moved in and there was quite a traffic to Troy because they had gone east to Bovill and Elk River. Bovill first and later Elk River. They had two liver barns at Troy and they had teens going out. They hauled people in supplies and everything.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Were they holding logs down through here too?

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: No. They logged up that way and worked apartments. They didn't come through here. There was a lot of traffic and that stimulated the business in town for quite a few years. Because there was quite a movement. But it's all in the days of horses. I never did work for them, but a lot of people around it worked for them. We kept digging away at farming. I did work on them. They were close a little bit.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Was Troy pretty law abiding?

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: Yes. For the early days I'd say it was pretty law abiding. There was one incident down there that when the town marshal went to arrest the party on the south side of town it was either in 1992 or 1994 and he tried to force his way in and this individual shot him.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: That was Marshal Hayes?

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: That was Marshal Hayes. He, of course, Hayes' cronies, well he had two boys they were going to mend up time. He got a few of them together and they were going to shoot this… they were going to shoot this ... on site. But the officials from Moscow come down and took him out the back way out of the hotel. So they never got a chance at him. He's playing sides. He didn't serve very many years so he got out. I don't know what to come with.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: I've heard that. Marshal Hayes was a pretty hard guy to get along with.

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: Oh yes, well he was kind of hard. Whether he had the right to go outside of town I don't know if some say it was because I guess across the track probably wasn't incorporated into town either. People had to dislike him that way.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: For quite a while there was quite a bit of mining up in this area too, wasn't there? Or prospecting?

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: There was prospecting north of town and some east of town about… 6, 7 miles east of town. They had the mine there. They called it the Copper Sheath. And then Olsen voice… and O .K. Olsen had one but… 3 .5 or 4 miles out of this canyon. Oh, they did it. They had tons of loose running in there and everything. They didn't really know anything they had developed really on the subject.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: They never had much success.

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: No, probably this day they could. That is all.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: You were telling me last time we were talking about was it your wife's grandad? Was it going to leave this country at one time?

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: Yeah, Paul Smith my wife's grandad. He… in 93 and 4 in there. He had been here since 83 and the depression come on and the crop got wet and one thing or another. So he decided to leave. He said he's going to leave in the new store at Moscow which is Dale's now. That name's been going for a long time but another outfit that owns it. They run that.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Who ran it?

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: Durham and Kaufman. Durham and Kaufman run that. They had given credit to let him around here and the hard times come on and one crop beer was wet. He would have been told that he's got to quit. He says I've got nothing close to wear and nothing to feed the family and no machinery to speak of but they told him no you're not going to leave well I can't stay I can't keep on. Finally they said we'll furnish everything you need and he said he tried again and they furnished him with what the family needed and anything else she needed and they told him now for him all the land you can and more too so he got some neighbors to help so he put in quite a bit of land and when that coming year and when he had harvested that beer and sold his crop he got five thousand dollars and it was in gold. So he came out fine anyhow.

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: He managed to pay his debts and buy a hundred and sixty acres for sixteen hundred dollars. Well they gave him all the food and everything else. He actually wasn't quite a predicament because he wore gunnies on his feet.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: They gave him a seed ring too.

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: He got his neighbors to help.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Did he pay his neighbors or did they just do a work exchange?

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: They paid it back and forth. I don't think they knew what was what. They did not have to carry the wrong thing.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: Do you think Durham-Kaufman helped bail out quite a few people?

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: Those that were willing to stick it out. Durham-Kaufman after some time sold out and went down to San Francisco and run a work in the business. But… people seemed to like that Durham-Kaufman. They were just interested in business. They weren't interested in land. They didn't want it.

speaker: Rob Moore
words: It sounds like they're also interested in helping the community out. Oh yes.

speaker: Clarence Johnson
words: They figured well to get someone to stay in the business. We collected some of it. They were different that way. Then the first one. Then like Vollmer… well now I tell you… that's about enough for me. Then you get those. You shut it off.
